title: Hummus: protein, fiber, fat and nutrition

seo.title: Hummus: protein, fiber, fat and calories
seo.meta_description: A current plain-hummus reference has 243 calories, 7.3 g protein, 5.4 g fiber and 17.1 g fat per 100 g. See what a 60 g serving provides.
seo.search_intent: Understand hummus nutrition and what a realistic serving contributes

excerpt: Hummus combines chickpeas with tahini and, depending on the recipe, oil, lemon, garlic and salt. A current USDA plain-hummus reference provides about 243 calories, 7.3 g protein, 5.4 g fiber and 17.1 g fat per 100 g. A 60 g portion works out to roughly 146 calories, 4.4 g protein, 3.2 g fiber and 10.3 g fat. Recipes can shift these values substantially.
content_html:
Hummus starts with chickpeas, but it is not just mashed chickpeas. Tahini and, in many recipes, added oil change the balance of fat and calories. It contributes protein and fiber, but it is also much fattier than cooked chickpeas alone.

What plain hummus provides

A current USDA survey reference for plain hummus contains per 100 g about 243 calories, 7.3 g protein, 17.1 g fat, 14.9 g carbohydrate and 5.4 g fiber.

NutrientPer 100 gPer 60 g
Calories243~146
Protein7.3 g~4.4 g
Fat17.1 g~10.3 g
Fiber5.4 g~3.2 g
Carbohydrate14.9 g~8.9 g

Sixty grams resembles a generous dip or spread serving. The protein contributes to a meal, but 4.4 g is very different from treating the 7.3 g per 100 g number as if it were automatically your serving.

Where does the fat come from?

Mainly from tahini and any added oil, with smaller contributions from chickpeas. In traditional formulations, much of that fat is unsaturated because sesame and olive or other plant oils are rich in unsaturated fatty acids.

More tahini or oil also means more energy, so two hummus recipes with similar chickpea content can differ substantially in calories.

Fiber still comes largely from chickpeas

Chickpeas contribute cell-wall fiber and resistant starch, while sesame adds some fiber too. At 5.4 g/100 g in the reference used here, a 60 g serving provides about 3.2 g.

Is hummus a high-protein food?

It is more accurate to say hummus contributes protein. A 60 g serving supplies about 4.4 g. Pairing hummus with whole grains and another protein-rich food can build a higher-protein meal; a thin swipe by itself is not equivalent to a bowl of beans.

Sodium is worth checking on the label

Commercial recipes use very different amounts of salt. If sodium matters to you, compare products per 100 g rather than assuming all hummus contains the same amount.

Hummus gets its nutrition from the combination: legume, sesame and plant fat. The recipe and serving size determine how much you actually get.

Hummus works best as part of a meal, not as a stand-alone protein food

The chickpeas in hummus provide protein and fiber, but the finished dip is diluted by tahini, oil, lemon juice and water. That is why a few tablespoons contain less protein than the same weight of cooked chickpeas. A normal serving can still make a meal more satisfying, especially when it replaces a sauce based mostly on refined fat or when it helps people eat more vegetables, but calling hummus a “high-protein food” can set unrealistic expectations. If protein is the goal, pair it with another source such as eggs, yogurt, chicken, tuna, tofu, edamame or additional legumes.

What you dip into hummus also changes the meal. Carrot, cucumber, pepper and radish add volume and fiber with relatively little energy, while pita or crackers provide more carbohydrate and can be perfectly appropriate depending on appetite and the rest of the day. A lunch built from hummus, whole-grain bread, vegetables and a clear protein source is nutritionally different from eating a large tub of hummus with handfuls of chips. Portion context matters because hummus contains sesame and often olive or other oil, making it more energy-dense than the vegetables served beside it.

Homemade and store-bought versions can differ mainly in sodium, fat and texture. At home, you can adjust salt, lemon, garlic, tahini and water to taste. Commercial hummus is convenient but worth comparing by the same serving size, especially if sodium intake matters. Sesame is also a major allergen in several countries, so tahini-containing hummus is not suitable for someone with a sesame allergy. The useful way to think about hummus is as a nutrient-dense spread or dip that contributes legumes, fiber and some protein while fitting into a broader meal rather than carrying the whole protein target by itself.

For a quick label comparison, put two brands side by side and normalize the serving size before judging them. One package may look lower in sodium simply because it lists a smaller serving, so comparing the same number of grams prevents that common mistake.

faq.question: How much protein is in hummus?
faq.answer: The reference used here contains 7.3 g/100 g, about 4.4 g in a 60 g serving.

faq.question: How much fiber is in hummus?
faq.answer: About 5.4 g/100 g, or roughly 3.2 g in 60 g.

faq.question: Why is hummus high in fat?
faq.answer: Tahini and added oil contribute much of the fat; most is typically unsaturated.

faq.question: Does all hummus have the same calories?
faq.answer: No. Chickpea, tahini, oil and water proportions can shift energy density substantially.
